extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the theory of reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing and constructing definitions, distinguishing definitions from postulates, and evaluating legitimate inferences (conversion, induction, syllogism) in formal and informal reasoning. Focuses on when propositions supply real proof versus mere verbal equivalence and on principles for good definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions concern names, not things
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions properly are of names only, and not of things; the only propositions that can be derived from a definition (taken strictly) are propositions about meanings of words, not about actual existence or properties of real things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Replace 'is' by 'means' in definitional premises to show they yield only verbal conclusions. Even when philosophers treat definitions as about ideas rather than things, the conclusions still ultimately rest on the postulate that the idea (not necessarily a real object) exists. Therefore, do not treat definitional statements as premises that assert facts about the external world unless an independent postulate of existence is supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not tacitly assume existence from a definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition does not by itself establish the real existence of an object conforming to that definition; treating a definition as asserting existence can lead to valid syllogisms with false conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: ‘A dragon is a serpent breathing flame’ is a correct definition of the word 'dragon' but does not justify asserting that any real serpent breathes flame. To avoid the error, explicit premises asserting real existence must be included when conclusions concern things. The text warns that taking definitions as premises about real objects yields the absurdity of true premises leading to a false conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When definitions are used in arguments, state the relevant postulate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a definitional premise is to serve in a demonstration about things, the argument must include the postulate that an object conformable to the definition may be made to exist (or does exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example with geometry: the ability to describe a circle about a centre with a given radius is a postulate (covert assumption) required for geometrical demonstrations — the definition alone is insufficient. Whether that postulate is grounded in intuition or proof is a separate question, but it must be explicit as the true premise on which theorems depend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform 'is' into 'means' to avoid category errors
rubrics_metrics.description: To see when a syllogistic conclusion is only about words, substitute 'means' for 'is' in definitional premises; the resulting syllogism will yield only verbal conclusions that are true but not factual about external objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example transformation: From 'Dragon is a word meaning a thing which breathes flame' and 'Dragon is a word meaning a serpent' infer 'Some word or words which mean a serpent, also mean a thing which breathes flame.' This shows the only legitimate conclusion from definitions concerns meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ideas from things in premises
rubrics_metrics.description: When the middle term names an idea rather than a thing or word, the premises assert psychological facts (existence of ideas) and conclusions about ideas follow legitimately; but if conclusions concern things, a postulate of real existence is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The idea of a dragon is an idea of a serpent' and 'The idea of a dragon is an idea of a thing which breathes flame' legitimately entail that there is an idea of a serpent which is an idea of a thing breathing flame. This shows the legitimacy of conclusions depends on the ontological type of the postulated subject (word, idea, thing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are not arbitrary; they should be tied to the nature of things
rubrics_metrics.description: Although definitions are definitions of names, crafting a good definition may require deep inquiry into the nature and properties of the things named; for difficult abstract names the definitional question often concerns what the name should mean, not just conventional usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical inquiries like 'What is justice?' or 'What is virtue?' are not mere terminological conventions but involve investigating the resemblances and causal bases of the things denoted. Thus, when forming definitions, consider empirical and conceptual investigations of the objects, not mere lexicographic fiat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve existing denotation when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing a distinct connotation for a general name, prefer meanings compatible with the name continuing to denote, if possible, most or the more important of the objects to which it is commonly applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry into a definition tacitly assumes one aims to keep the name applicable to the greater or more important portion of the commonly denoted things. If no common resemblance runs through all instances, determine the largest subclass that does share a general resemblance and define the name accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select differentiæ that yield important and interesting propriae
rubrics_metrics.description: In giving a distinct connotation, the philosopher should select such differentiæ (distinguishing attributes) as are common to the things denoted and of greatest importance — those that lead to many interesting proprietary properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor conspicuous, numerous, or consequence-rich attributes rather than obscure qualities on which the obvious resemblances depend. This strategy makes the resulting class scientifically and philosophically fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair overextended or vague names by restricting denotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a name has by successive extensions come to denote a confused huddle of objects and predicates nothing definite, it must be narrowed (given a distinct connotation) to objects sharing some definite attributes to be useful for thought and communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An overextended name that asserts nothing should be made serviceable by stripping some of its multifarious denotation and confining it to a subset with common attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical/established usage as evidence in definitional work
rubrics_metrics.description: The spontaneous growth of language yields customary classifications that, although imperfect, contain useful material and indicate resemblances that have struck many persons over time; these are evidence to be considered when revising definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established groupings are like customary law — less perfect than systematic codes but often practically suited to the logician's purposes. Transitions in a word's meaning may reveal hidden connections worth investigating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent inference (equipollency) is not genuine reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conclusion is merely a restatement or part of what is already asserted in the premise (equipollency or conversion cases), there is no real inference and no new proof is obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include rewordings (No man is incapable of reason for every man is rational), deriving a particular from a universal (All A is B therefore Some A is B), or asserting a predicate that is already connoted by the original predicate (Socrates is a man therefore Socrates is a living creature). Recognize and exclude such cases from accounts of genuine inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and apply conversion rules correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion operations allow forming equivalent or partly equivalent propositions by reversing subject and predicate, but each form has strict limits (simple conversion, conversion per accidens, contraposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules and examples given: Some A is B => Some B is A (simple conversion); All A is B cannot be converted to All B is A but converts per accidens to Some B is A; No A is B => No B is A (simple conversion); Some A is not B converts (by contraposition) into 'something which is not B is A' after suitable reformulation. Be careful not to infer stronger claims than conversion permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse conversion per accidens with full converse
rubrics_metrics.description: From All A is B one cannot infer All B is A; at best one can infer Some B is A (conversion per accidens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'All water is liquid' does not imply 'All liquid is water' but does allow 'Some liquid is water.' Be explicit about whether a converse is universal or particular when assessing inference strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate induction and ratiocination (syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is inferring a proposition more general than the premises (from particulars to generals); ratiocination or syllogism is inferring a proposition equally or less general than the premises (from generals to particulars or to equally general propositions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational characterization: induction ascends from observed instances to laws; ratiocination combines general propositions to derive individual or less-general conclusions. Note the author also signals a third species of reasoning that underlies both, to be discussed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define proof as belief grounded on other propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is proved when we believe its truth by reason of some other fact or statement from which it is said to follow; inference is granting credence to a conclusion on the ground of prior accepted truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most propositions we accept are inferred rather than directly known. The text frames logic's task as explaining how assertions analyzed earlier are proved or disproved, focusing on those not amenable to direct consciousness or intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn logical opposition and its practical value
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity with the opposition of propositions (contrary, contradictory, subcontrary, subalternate) is a technical tool that helps detect identity and differences of assertions framed in different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though these axioms may seem technical, they cultivate habits of precise interpretation and are useful in rapidly recognizing whether apparently different statements are logically equivalent, inconsistent, or entail one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the habit of discerning identity under varied wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Training in recognizing the same assertion disguised by different language is one of the chief intellectual gains of logical study and is essential to sound reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends exercises in conversion and equipollency for students to develop circumspect interpretation and accurate measurement of their assertions' scope — a habit critical across intellectual disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept idealization in postulates if sufficient for conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates used in demonstrative sciences (e.g., exact equality of radii of a circle) may be idealizations not literally true in nature, but as much of the postulate as is true is sufficient to support as much of the conclusion as is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that mathematical or geometrical premises can be ideal and still validly support conclusions about real objects to the extent those idealized premises are instantiated. Philosophical concern about exact physical instantiation should not be confused with the logical role of the postulate.
